title: Remark
body_md: The formulas in~\eqref{eq:nonparametric_est} and~\eqref{eq:pv} naturally allow for a continuity correction in the case of ties: If $\hat \theta$ is defined by $\hat \theta = \sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1} \sum_{i_2=1}^{n_2} ( 1\{T_{1i_1} > T_{2i_2}\} + 0.5 \cdot 1\{T_{1i_1} = T_{2i_2}\} )/ (n_1 n_2)$, it is easy to see that $\tilde \theta_{i_1 i_2} = 1\{T_{1i_1} > T_{2i_2}\} + 0.5 \cdot 1\{T_{1i_1} = T_{2i_2}\} $.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The definition in~\eqref{eq:pv} seems to be in contrast to \citet[p.~15]{efron79} who stated that not pairs of observations should be left out but rather all observations of both samples consecutively, without such pairings.
Efron's arguments are based on two related papers \citep{miller74, hinkley77} which both considered linear regression problems.
Some authors indeed apply the one-sample jackknife to both samples consecutively, also in censored data problems; see e.g.\ \cite{chang12}.
On the other hand, \cite{schewa04} proposed the two-sample jackknife as applied in~\eqref{eq:pv}. \cite{chuang12} applied this type of two-sample jackknife method to the Jaccard index.

label: rem:finite_tau
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:finite_tau}
In practice, longitudinal studies typically end after a finite time horizon, say $\tau >0$, before all events could have occurred.
This renders the right tail of the survival functions unidentifiable.
As a solution, there are mathematical approaches that allow the survival and censoring distributions to have the same (finite or infinite) support under stricter assumptions on the censoring distribution \citep{gill83,ying89,dobler19}.

One solution for the presently considered estimand $\theta$ is to instead use $\hat \theta(\tau) = - \int_0^\tau \hat S_1(u) d \hat S_2(u) $, which is a consistent estimator for $\theta(\tau) = P(\min(T_{1i_1},\tau) > \min(T_{2i_2}, \tau))$
if $P(T_{2i_2}=\tau)=0$. We will consider the estimand $\theta(\tau)$ and its estimator $\hat \theta(\tau)$ in the remainder of this paper. This is analogous to the Cox model where a time horizon $\tau$ should be chosen before computing the maximizer of the partial likelihood.

title: Remark
body_md:
In the special case of fully observable data, $\tilde \theta_{i_1i_2} = 1\{T_{1i_1} > T_{2i_2}\}$, it is easy to verify Assumptions~\ref{ass:general}.2--\ref{ass:general}.5. 
    To see this, let us assume that $\mu$ is three times continuously differentiable and that the second moments of $\boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2}$ and $\boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2}(\tilde \theta_{i_1i_2} - \mu_{i_1 i_2})$ exist for all $\boldsymbol \beta \in \mathbb R^p$.
    The postulated assumptions are then consequences of laws of large numbers and a central limit theorem for two-sample $U$-statistics.
    
    For example, after noticing that $\text{E}(\tilde \theta_{i_1i_2} | \boldsymbol Z_{i_1}, \boldsymbol Z_{i_2}) = \mu_{i_1i_2}$,
    the Jacobian $D \boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0) $ reduces to 
    $$-\frac1{n_1n_2}\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1} \sum_{i_2=1}^{n_2} \boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2} \boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2}^\top + o_p(1) ,$$ 
    which converges in probability to $- \boldsymbol \Sigma(\boldsymbol \beta_0) = - \text{E}(\boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2} \boldsymbol A_{i_1i_2}^\top)$ by the strong law of large numbers for multi-sample $U$-statistics, e.g., Theorem~3.2.1 in \cite{kobo94}.
    It remains to assume that $- \boldsymbol \Sigma(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ does not have a zero eigenvalue. Similarly, 
                                                                                                                                        
    the local uniformity of the convergence in Assumption~\ref{ass:general}.4 follows from the continuous differentiability of $D\boldsymbol U$ in~$\boldsymbol \beta_0$ and the pointwise convergence at each $\boldsymbol\beta$.
The existence of the stationary point $\boldsymbol \beta_0$ of the limiting function $f$ is ensured by the unbiasedness of~$\boldsymbol U$ at the true $\boldsymbol \beta = \boldsymbol \beta_0$ and the law of large numbers, from which it follows that $\boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0) \stackrel{a.s.} {\longrightarrow} \boldsymbol 0 = \text{E}(\boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0)) = \nabla f (\boldsymbol \beta_0) $. Finally, the convergence in distribution in Assumption~\ref{ass:general}.5  follows from a central limit theorem for $U$-statistics; cf.\@ Theorem~4.5.1 in \cite{kobo94}.

title: Remark
body_md:
Based on Assumption~\ref{ass:general} and the consistency of $\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$ for $\boldsymbol \beta_0$, a consistent estimator for $-\check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ is given by
    $$ \widehat{D \boldsymbol U}(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}) := \frac1{n_1n_2} \sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1} \sum_{i_2=1}^{n_2} \Big(\boldsymbol Z_{i_1i_2} \boldsymbol Z_{i_1i_2}^\top \, \mu''(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}^\top \boldsymbol Z_{i_1i_2}) \,(\tilde \theta_{i_1i_2} - \hat{\mu}_{i_1 i_2} ) - \hat{\boldsymbol A}_{i_1i_2} \hat{\boldsymbol A}_{i_1i_2}^\top \Big),$$
    where $\hat{\boldsymbol A}_{i_1i_2}$ and $\hat{\mu}_{i_1 i_2} $ are defined in the same way as ${\boldsymbol A}_{i_1i_2}$ and ${\mu}_{i_1 i_2} $, respectively, with $\boldsymbol \beta$ replaced by $\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$.
    As in \cite{ovpape17}, we expect the limiting distribution to depend on a second derivative of the functional which produces the estimators $\hat \theta$ based on the nonparametric estimators $\hat S_1, \hat S_2$.
For this reason, we introduced another notation for $\check{\boldsymbol \Omega}$, in order to distinguish it from~$\boldsymbol \Omega$ in the uncensored case. In contrast to $\check{\boldsymbol \Omega}$, $\boldsymbol \Omega$ does not depend on such second derivative.
For practical applications, we propose to use a group-wise bootstrap procedure, {\color{black}i.e., randomly drawing with replacement from the original data points within each group,} instead of implementing an estimator of $\check{\boldsymbol \Omega}$. We will pursue this approach in the simulation study in Section~\ref{sec:simus} below.
In the uncensored case, it is fairly straightforward to estimate $\boldsymbol \Omega$ by an appropriate empirical estimator, as explained in Appendix \ref{app:proofs}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first note that the expectation of $\hat {\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ equals
$$ \boldsymbol \Sigma = \text{E} \Big(\Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big)\Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix} \Big)^\top \Big). $$
By the law of large numbers applied to each of the two samples, it is easy to see that $\boldsymbol \Sigma$ is the almost sure limit of $\hat {\boldsymbol \Sigma}$ (since both $\boldsymbol Z_{1i}$ and $\boldsymbol Z_{2j}$ have finite second moments by assumption).

Similarly, the expectation of $\hat{\boldsymbol \Psi}$ equals
$$ \boldsymbol \Psi = \text{E} \Big( \Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{11} > T_{21} \} \Big) , $$
which could be slightly simplified using the independence of the two samples.
Also note that the first entry equals the unconditional Mann-Whitney effect $\theta$. By definition, $\hat{\boldsymbol \Psi}$ has the structure of a $U$-statistic which is similar to the Mann-Whitney $U$-statistic.
As a consequence, classical theory for $U$-statistics (e.g., Theorem~4.5.1 of \citealp{kobo94}) in combination with Slutsky's theorem 
implies that
$$\boldsymbol  \Omega_{n_1n_2}^{-1/2}(\hat{\boldsymbol \Psi} - \boldsymbol \Psi) \stackrel d \to \mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol 0, \boldsymbol I_p) , $$
provided that the matrix
\begin{align}
\begin{split}
\label{eq:omega}
 \boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2} \, & = \, a_{n_1n_2} \boldsymbol \Omega^{(0)} + b_{n_1n_2} \boldsymbol \Omega^{(1)} + c_{n_1n_2} \boldsymbol \Omega^{(2)} \\
  & := \frac1{n_1n_2} 
 \text{var}\Big(\Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{11} > T_{21} \} \Big) \\
 & \phantom{:=} + \frac{n_2-1}{n_1n_2} \, \text{cov}\Big(\Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{11} > T_{21} \}, \Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{22} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{11} > T_{22} \} \Big) \\
 & \phantom{:=} + \frac{n_1-1}{n_1n_2} \, \text{cov}\Big(\Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{11} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{11} > T_{21} \}, \Big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ \boldsymbol Z_{12} \\ \boldsymbol Z_{21} \end{smallmatrix}\Big) 1\{T_{12} > T_{21} \} \Big) 
\end{split}
\end{align}
has full rank. Here, $\boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2}^{-1/2} := (\boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2}^{1/2})^{-1}$, where the square root is defined by the positive definite matrix satisfying $\boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2}^{1/2} \boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2}^{1/2} = \boldsymbol \Omega_{n_1n_2}$. Finally, using $n_1/(n_1+n_2) \to \lambda \in (0,1)$
as well as 
$$ \sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}} \, \hat {\boldsymbol \Sigma}^{-1}\hat {\boldsymbol \Psi} = \hat {\boldsymbol \Sigma}^{-1} \Big( \frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2} \, \boldsymbol\Omega_{n_1n_2}\Big)^{1/2} \Big(\boldsymbol\Omega_{n_1n_2}^{-1/2} \hat {\boldsymbol \Psi}  \Big), $$
the previous results combined with Slutsky's theorem yield
$$ \sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}} \, (\hat {\boldsymbol \beta} - \boldsymbol \beta_0) = \sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}} \, (\hat {\boldsymbol \Sigma}^{-1}\hat {\boldsymbol \Psi} - \boldsymbol \Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol \Psi) \, \stackrel d \to \, \mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol 0, \boldsymbol \Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol \Omega (\boldsymbol \Sigma^{-1})^\top) $$
as $\min(n_1,n_2) \to \infty$, where $\boldsymbol \Omega = (1-\lambda) \boldsymbol \Omega^{(1)} + \lambda \boldsymbol \Omega^{(2)}$. \hfill \qed

name: the central limit theorem in Example \refex:identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $- \check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta)$ is negative definite and continuous in $\boldsymbol \beta_0$, it is also negative definite on the open ball $B = B_\varepsilon(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ of some radius $\varepsilon > 0$ around $\boldsymbol \beta_0$. This is because the largest eigenvalue of $- \check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta)$ changes continuously with $\boldsymbol \beta$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ be small enough so that the largest eigenvalue of all $- \check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta)$, $\boldsymbol \beta \in B$, is bounded away from~0, and such that the assumed uniform convergence of $D\boldsymbol U$ to $-\check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}$ in probability holds on $B$.
As a consequence, the event that the biggest eigenvalue of $D\boldsymbol U$ is negative has a probability converging to 1 as $\min(n_1,n_2)\to \infty$. Hence it is no restriction to consider all arguments in the remainder of this proof conditionally on the event
$$D_{n_1n_2}(\varepsilon) := \{D\boldsymbol U (\boldsymbol \beta) \text{ is negative definite for all } \boldsymbol \beta \in B_{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)\}.$$

Using the arguments from \cite{angi82}, Appendix~II, the maximum of $\boldsymbol \beta \mapsto C(\boldsymbol \beta)$ (over the compact subset $\overline{B_{\varepsilon/2}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)}$, i.e., the closed ball) converges to the maximizing value of $C$ in probability, i.e., to $\boldsymbol \beta_0$.
 Now Corollary~II.2 of \cite{angi82} implies that the maximizer $\hat {\boldsymbol \beta}$ of $C$ eventually lies in the open set $B_{\varepsilon/2}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ in probability, i.e., it is a stationary point of $\boldsymbol U$. Consequently, the probability that the root of $\boldsymbol U$ exists tends to 1.
For these arguments we also used that $\boldsymbol \beta_0$ is the only root of $\nabla f$ and that $C$ converges pointwise in probability to $f$. In combination with Corollary~II.2 of \cite{angi82}, it follows from $\boldsymbol \beta_0$ being the only stationary point of $f$ that $\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$ exists with a probability tending to~1.

Now, applying the mean value theorem individually to each component $U_k(\boldsymbol \beta)$, $k=1, \dots, p$, of $\boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta)$, there exist points $\boldsymbol \beta_k$ on the line segment between $\boldsymbol \beta_0$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$ such that 
$$U_k(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}) - U_k(\boldsymbol \beta_0) = \nabla U_k(\boldsymbol \beta_k) (\hat{\boldsymbol \beta} - \boldsymbol \beta_0). $$
Denote by $\widetilde {D \boldsymbol U}(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}, \boldsymbol \beta_0) $ the matrix consisting of the rows $\nabla U_k(\boldsymbol \beta_k), k=1, \dots, p$.
Then, by the existence of the root $\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$ of $\boldsymbol U$, it follows that 
$$ - \boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0) = \widetilde{D \boldsymbol U} (\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}, \boldsymbol \beta_0) \, (\hat{\boldsymbol \beta} - \boldsymbol \beta_0). $$
The matrix $\widetilde{D \boldsymbol U}(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}, \boldsymbol \beta_0)$ is invertible due to conditioning on the set $D_{n_1n_2}(\varepsilon)$.
The uniform convergence of $D \boldsymbol U$ to $- \check{ \boldsymbol \Sigma} $ in probability over $B_{\varepsilon/2}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ and the continuity of the limit in $\boldsymbol \beta_0$ yield 
$\widetilde{D \boldsymbol U}(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}, \boldsymbol \beta_0) \stackrel p \to - \check{ \boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$.
Combining these arguments, using the assumed central limit theorem for $\boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0)$ postulated in Assumption~\ref{ass:general}.5, and using Slutsky's theorem, we obtain
\begin{align*}
                   
    \sqrt{\frac{n_1n_2}{n_1+n_2}}\, (\hat{\boldsymbol \beta} - \boldsymbol \beta_0) \, = \, - \sqrt{\frac{n_1n_2}{n_1+n_2}} \, (\widetilde {D \, \boldsymbol U}(\hat{\boldsymbol \beta}, \boldsymbol \beta_0) )^{-1} \boldsymbol U(\boldsymbol \beta_0) \, \stackrel d \to \, \check{\boldsymbol \Sigma}(\boldsymbol \beta_0) \boldsymbol W
\end{align*}
as $\min(n_1,n_2) \to \infty$, with the claimed multivariate normal distribution.
